title: Sum an Array Without Overflowing
statement:
Java arrays are fixed-size and, unlike a `List`, hold primitive `int`s
directly -- no boxing, no autoboxing overhead, just a contiguous block of
32-bit values. Summing them is the plainest possible loop, and the whole
exercise is choosing the right type to hold the running total.

## Your function

```
public static long sumArray(int[] values);
```

Return the sum of every element of `values`. `values` may be empty, in
which case the sum is `0`.

## Watch out

- **The return type is `long`, not `int`.** `values` can hold enough
  large `int` elements that their true sum does not fit in 32 bits, even
  though every individual element does. Accumulate into the `long` the
  return type already commits you to from the very first addition -- not
  into an `int` total you only widen at the end, by which point an
  overflow has already happened. Java's `int` arithmetic never throws on
  overflow; it wraps silently to a nonsense value and keeps going.
- **`int` array elements do not automatically become `long` during
  addition just because the total is a `long`.** `total += values[i]` is
  fine -- the compiler widens `values[i]` to `long` for that specific
  addition -- but a running total that is itself declared `int` never
  gets that help, because the widening only happens once, at the point of
  the addition into an already-`long` variable.
- An empty array's sum is `0`, not an error -- a loop that simply never
  executes its body already produces the right answer.

tests.name: an empty array sums to zero
a sum that overflows a 32-bit int but not a 64-bit long
tests.description: 6,000,000,000 is past Integer.MAX_VALUE (~2.1 billion) -- accumulating into a 32-bit int silently wraps to a negative number instead of throwing.
